title: Challenges in Information-Seeking QA: Unanswerable Questions and Paragraph Retrieval
research_question: Why do naturally occurring information-seeking questions remain unanswerable for strong QA systems, and how much of the difficulty comes from paragraph selection, answerability prediction, missing evidence, invalid questions, or restrictive task design?
methodology: The paper analyzes Natural Questions and TyDi QA, contrasting their naturally occurring information-seeking queries with SQuAD 2.0's artificially constructed unanswerable questions. It performs controlled oracle experiments that provide models with gold answer type and/or gold evidence paragraphs, then evaluates answerability classification using question-only and full QA models. The authors manually classify 800 unanimously unanswerable examples from NQ and five TyDi languages, search alternative Wikipedia and non-Wikipedia sources, and categorize failures into retrieval misses, non-factoid or multi-evidence needs, invalid questions, false premises, and annotation errors. Performance is reported with QA F1/precision/recall, answer-type classification accuracy, category-level error rates, and annotation agreement.

key_findings.finding: Oracle experiments show that paragraph selection and answerability prediction account for substantial remaining error; once models receive gold evidence and answer-type information, their answer extraction becomes much stronger.
key_findings.section: 3 QA performances with Gold Answer Type and Gold Paragraph

key_findings.finding: Answerability prediction remains difficult on naturally occurring information-seeking questions: for binary classification, the reported QA model reaches 82.5% on NQ and 79.4% on TyDi QA, compared with aggregate human agreement of 85.6% and 94.0%.

Question-only models exceed 70% binary answerability accuracy on NQ and TyDi QA, showing that surface-form artifacts provide substantial cues even though the questions were collected independently of evidence documents.

The causes of unanswerability vary strongly by dataset and language: 38% of the analyzed NQ unanswerable subset consists of invalid or ill-defined questions, whereas retrieval misses account for roughly 50-74% of annotated TyDi examples across the five studied languages.

Many questions labeled unanswerable relative to their supplied document become answerable when annotators search another Wikipedia page or a non-Wikipedia source, demonstrating that evidence-source coverage is a major determinant of apparent answerability.
Single-paragraph extractive task definitions themselves create unanswerability for questions that require multiple pieces of evidence or descriptive, non-factoid answers.
Lexically related but incorrect evidence can induce confident wrong answers, so evidence relevance alone is insufficient for reliable abstention.

limitations: The primary modeling experiments use a reading-comprehension setting with a supplied reference document rather than a fully adaptive open-domain retrieval controller.
The manual study contains 800 examples and covers NQ plus five TyDi languages, so it is not a comprehensive sample of all information-seeking domains or languages.
The categorization boundaries can overlap, particularly between retrieval failure and inherently multi-evidence or non-factoid questions.
Searching heterogeneous non-Wikipedia sources improves coverage but introduces untested domain-adaptation and format-generalization problems.
The paper identifies abstention and evidence-coverage problems but does not implement a calibrated risk-bounded stopping policy.
It does not model temporal validity, document versions, or permission-aware retrieval.
The authors note that moving from extractive to free-form answers creates a harder evaluation problem that the study does not solve.
raw_claims: Naturally occurring information-seeking QA remains harder than reading-comprehension benchmarks whose questions are written from the evidence.
Providing gold evidence paragraphs and gold answer types removes a large fraction of model errors.
Predicting whether a question is answerable remains a major source of error.
Question-only classifiers can exploit cues in the wording of NQ and TyDi questions.
The reasons questions are unanswerable differ substantially across datasets and languages.
Ill-defined questions form a large part of the unanswerable Natural Questions sample.
Document-retrieval failures dominate several of the analyzed TyDi language subsets.
Some apparently unanswerable factoid questions have answers on different Wikipedia pages or non-Wikipedia websites.
Some questions require information distributed across multiple paragraphs or documents.
A single-paragraph extractive formulation can incorrectly convert a valid information need into an unanswerable example.
Models can give high-confidence wrong answers when an irrelevant paragraph has misleading lexical overlap with the query.
The authors recommend broader knowledge sources, clarification of ambiguous questions, multi-document access, and abstractive answering.
The paper's code and annotated data are publicly available.
